claim: White noise (WN) at 90 dB is aversive to rats, as demonstrated by significantly reduced time spent in a WN-paired quadrant (9.71 ± 1.65%) compared to chance level (25%) in a real-time place aversion test.
source: On average, rats (n = 10) spent a significantly smaller percentage of time in the WN quadrant (9.71 ± 1.65) compared to chance level (t(9) = 9.585, p<0.0001; Figure 1A, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral testing showing statistical significance (t-test, p<0.0001) and visual representation in Figure 1A.

claim: When 90 dB WN was paired with a rat's preferred quadrant, rats spent significantly less time in that quadrant compared to when no WN was present.
source: After this session, rats were placed in the open field in a second session, where now the entry into their preferred quadrant led to 90 dB WN exposure (Figure 1B, middle panel), which caused the rats to spend significantly less time in it (no WN: 48.5 ± 0.2474, 90 dB: 7.983 ± 0.3875, t(14) = 13.43, p<0.0001; Figure 1B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing statistical significance (t(14) = 13.43, p<0.0001) and Figure 1B visualization.

claim: WN aversiveness is dose-dependent, with higher WN intensities causing rats to spend less time foraging for food pellets.
source: The greater the WN intensity, the shorter the amount of time rats spent foraging for food pellets (χ2(5) = 27.6, p<0.0001), whereas the tone did not reduce foraging (Figure 1C, middle panel)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from foraging task with statistical analysis (chi-square test, p<0.0001) and Figure 1C.

claim: WN is more aversive than a pure tone of the same decibel level.
source: whereas the tone did not reduce foraging (Figure 1C, middle panel), indicating that WN is more aversive than a pure tone (t(10) = 2.389, p=0.0381).
evidence: Supported by comparative experimental data with statistical significance (t(10) = 2.389, p=0.0381).

claim: Rats' behavioral response to different WN intensities is reliable across multiple sessions, demonstrating absence of sensitization or habituation.
source: The rats' response to the different WN intensities and the tone was reliable across first and second sessions (Figure 1C, right panel), demonstrating the absence of sensitization or habituation of the behavioral response to WN across sessions and days.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations across multiple sessions shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WN exposure stimulates locomotor activity in rats in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, exposure to WN stimulated locomotor activity: rats in an operant box significantly increased locomotion speed in response to semi-random presentation of 6 s WN bouts (t(13) = 7.059, p<0.0001; Figure 1D, middle panel). This locomotor response was WN-intensity dependent as we found a main effect of intensity on baseline-subtracted locomotion speed (χ2(3) = 13.80, p=0.0032) in another cohort of rats (n = 13), and significant differences between 70 and 90 dB (p=0.005) and 70 and 96 dB (p=0.0143) (Figure 1D, right panel)
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance (t(13) = 7.059, p<0.0001; χ2(3) = 13.80, p=0.0032) and Figure 1D.

claim: Rats can discriminate between different magnitudes of WN, preferring lower intensity WN when given a choice.
source: Unsurprisingly, rats (n = 6) preferred the non-WN lever as indicated by a significant main effect of WN intensity using a Friedman test (χ2(3) = 11.57, p=0.0003). Importantly, when comparing the WN-paired lever presses, rats significantly preferred the 70 dB WN to the 96 dB WN (post-hoc Dunn's tests, p=0.0027; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from operant choice task with statistical analysis (Friedman test, χ2(3) = 11.57, p=0.0003; Dunn's test, p=0.0027).

claim: Unexpected exposure to 90 dB WN strongly and reliably decreases extracellular concentrations of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens core (NAC).
source: Unexpected exposure to 6 s of 90 dB WN strongly and reliably decreased extracellular concentrations of dopamine in the NAC (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by FSCV measurements shown in Figure 1H.

claim: WN decreases dopamine concentration in the NAC as an unconditioned response, observable from the first trial.
source: Post-hoc analyses using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with a Holm–Bonferroni multiple-comparison correction revealed significantly lower dopamine concentrations during the WN epoch compared to pre-cue baseline during trial 1 (Z = –1.988, p=0.0235), trial 2 (Z = –2.430, p=0.0075), trial 3 (Z = –2.327, p=0.010), trial 5 (Z = –3.464, p<0.0005), trials 6–10 (Z = 3.103, p=0.001), and trials 11–30 (Z = –3.516, p<0.0001), indicating that the decrease in dopamine during WN is an unconditioned response, since it is observed already during the first trial.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data across multiple trials with significance values provided.

claim: The WN-predictive cue acquires the ability to decrease dopamine concentration as a conditioned response, developing over time.
source: In contrast, we only observed significantly lower dopamine in the cue epoch compared to pre-cue baseline during trial 5 (Z = –1.965, p=0.0245), trials 6–10 (Z = –2.999, p=0.0015), and trials 11–30 (Z = –3.516, p<0.0001), indicating that this decrease develops over time and, therefore, is a conditioned response.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data showing temporal development of the response.

claim: WN does not provoke a substantial temporal shift of NAC dopamine signaling from unconditioned to conditioned cue within the first 30 trials of training.
source: In these first 30 trials, the decrease in extracellular dopamine during the WN epoch did not disappear or decrease. Thus, WN does not provoke a substantial temporal shift of NAC dopamine signaling from unconditioned to conditioned (predictive) cue within the first session of training.
evidence: Based on analysis of FSCV data showing persistent dopamine decrease during WN across trials.

claim: During aversive conditioning, the ratio of dopamine response between US and CS changes significantly between early day 1 trials and later trials, but not between late day 1 and day 6.
source: During aversive conditioning, we found, using a mixed-effects analysis, a significant main effect of the degree of conditioning (F(0.9586, 2.396) = 117.3, p=0.0043), and post-hoc testing using Tukey's multiple-comparisons test reveals significant differences between the ratios of day 1 early trials and day 1 later trials (p=0.0138), as well as between day 1 early trials and day 6 (p=0.0318). However, no difference was observed between day 1 later trials and day 6 (p=0.9852).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data with mixed-effects analysis and post-hoc testing.

claim: During appetitive conditioning, an almost complete shift of the dopamine response from the CS to the US occurs, unlike in aversive conditioning.
source: However, during appetitive conditioning, but not during aversive conditioning, an almost complete shift of the dopamine response from the CS to the US occurred. Together, these results demonstrate distinct differences in the temporal dynamics of dopamine signaling during aversive and appetitive conditioning.
evidence: Based on comparison of FSCV data between aversive and appetitive conditioning paradigms.

claim: Locomotion speed during cue presentation and WN exposure increases from day 1 to day 6 of aversive conditioning.
source: Left: during aversive conditioning, locomotion speed during cue presentation increased from day 1 to day 6 (Z = – 2.485, p=0.013), and also during WN (Z = –2.343, p=0.019) (n = 17).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data with statistical significance and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During appetitive conditioning, time spent in proximity of the reward magazine increases between days 1 and 6 both during cue presentation and after pellet delivery.
source: Right: during appetitive conditioning, time spent in proximity of the reward magazine increased between days 1 and 6 both during cue presentation (t(9) = 6.962, p<0.0001) and after pellet delivery (t(9) = 2.572, p=0.0301), (n = 10).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data with statistical significance and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The cue-induced decrease in dopamine concentration is stable between days 5 and 9, while WN-induced decrease is stable between days 1, 5, and 9.
source: Cue-induced decrease was stable between days 5 and 9, and WN-induced decrease was stable between days 1, 5, and 9 (n = 6, cue: F(1.428, 7.141) = 9.402, p=0.0133; day 1 vs. day 5: p=0.0035; day 1 vs. day 9: p=0.0882; day 5 vs. day 9: 0.7916; WN: F (1.236, 6.178) = 0.03898, p=0.8936; Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data across multiple days with significance values provided.

claim: Over the course of 15 extinction trials, the cue loses its conditioned dopamine response.
source: Post-hoc analysis using a Dunn's multiple-comparison test revealed a significant difference between the decrease in extracellular dopamine concentration of trials 1–5 and trials 16–20 (p=0.0133, Figure 2E), with the latter no longer showing a decrease in dopamine. Thus, over the course of 15 extinction trials, the cue lost its conditioned dopamine response.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data during extinction trials and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Extracellular dopamine in the NAC does not encode WN intensity, as different WN intensities (70, 80, 90, 96 dB) do not produce significantly different dopamine responses.
source: Although all WN intensities decreased dopamine release, we found no significant effect of intensity on extracellular dopamine (F(2.380, 11.90) = 0.1655, p=0.8813).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data comparing different WN intensities.

claim: Two different cues predicting 80 dB or 96 dB WN do not produce significantly different dopamine responses during either the cue or WN epochs.
source: Again, no significant differences were found in extracellular dopamine release between WN intensities (Z = –0.178, p=0.859), nor between the effects of their respective predicting cues (Z = –0.059, p=0.953).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of FSCV data comparing two different WN intensities and their cues.

claim: The relative aversiveness or aversive value of WN is not encoded by NAC dopamine.
source: Both of these experiments indicate that extracellular dopamine in the NAC does not encode WN intensity, and, therefore, the relative aversiveness or aversive value of WN is not encoded by NAC dopamine.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of dopamine response differences to varying WN intensities despite behavioral evidence of discrimination.

claim: There is no correlation between locomotion speed and extracellular dopamine concentration during cue and WN epochs on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: We performed a trial-by-trial analysis for both 80 dB (Figure 2H, top) and 96 dB (Figure 2H, bottom) WN exposures and found no correlation during the cue (80 dB: R2 = 0.0004, p=0.7223; 96 dB: R2 = 0.0003, p=0.7360) nor during WN (80 dB: R2 = 0.0016, p=0.4578; 96 dB: R2 = 0.0011, p=0.5374).
evidence: Supported by regression analysis of FSCV and behavioral data with R-squared values and p-values provided.

claim: The prediction error of outcomes deviating from expected probability is not encoded by NAC dopamine concentrations in a probabilistic task.
source: However, during the WN epoch, we also did not find significant differences between the two intensities, neither for tone 1 (t(8) = 0.6698, p=0.5218), nor for tone 2 (t(8) = 0.4452, p=0.6680). Together, these results indicate that the prediction error of outcomes deviating from expected probability is not encoded by NAC dopamine concentrations.
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of FSCV data in probabilistic conditioning paradigm showing no significant differences.

claim: During worse-than-predicted WN trials (12 s instead of 6 s), dopamine suppression extends at the same rate and ceases immediately upon WN termination.
source: During the worse-than-predicted WN trials where the WN was extended by 6 s, we observed an extended suppression of dopamine, which decreased at the same rate as during the initial 6 s, and which ceased immediately upon termination of WN, resulting in a overall lower dopamine concentration in the 11–25 s epoch (Figure 3D; t(10) = 1.863, p=0.046, after Holm–Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: Supported by FSCV measurements during extended WN trials with statistical analysis.

claim: During better-than-predicted trials (omitted WN), overall higher concentrations of dopamine are observed in the 5–20 s epoch.
source: During better-than-predicted trials (omitted WN), we found overall higher concentrations of dopamine in the 5–20 s epoch (Figure 3E; t(10) = 3.751, p=0.0019, after Holm–Bonferroni correction).
evidence: Supported by FSCV measurements during WN omission trials with statistical analysis.

claim: Unpredicted WN results in significantly lower dopamine concentrations exclusively in the epoch after WN termination, not during the WN epoch itself.
source: For the unpredicted WN, which constitutes a prediction error since the predictive cue is lacking, we aligned dopamine concentrations for predicted and unpredicted WN at its onset, in order to compare the impact of WN per se. We observed significantly lower dopamine concentrations exclusively in the epoch after the termination of the WN (Figure 3F; 11–25 s, t(10) = 2.453, p=0.0170, after Holm–Bonferroni correction), but not during the WN epoch itself.
evidence: Supported by FSCV measurements comparing predicted and unpredicted WN with statistical analysis.

claim: There is no significant slope difference in dopamine recovery between fully predicted WN trials and worse-than-expected trials.
source: Specifically, we found no significant slope difference between fully predicted WN trials and 'worse-than-expected' trials (t(10) = 0.1511, p=0.4415, after Holm–Bonferroni correction, Figure 3D, bar graph)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of dopamine recovery slopes in FSCV data.

claim: There is no significant slope difference in dopamine recovery between fully predicted WN trials and better-than-expected trials.
source: or 'better-than-expected' trials (t(10) = 0.4809, p=0.3205, after Holm–Bonferroni correction, Figure 3E, bar graph).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of dopamine recovery slopes in FSCV data.

claim: There is a significant difference in recovery slope between unexpected and expected WN, indicating dopamine may serve as a qualitative teaching signal.
source: In contrast, we found a significant difference in recovery slope between unexpected and expected WN (t(10) = 2.895, p=0.0080, after Holm–Bonferroni correction, Figure 3F, bar graph), which indicates that, in the case of an unexpected aversive stimulus, dopamine does not only track the duration of this aversive stimulus, but displays a differential response and, thus, may serve as a qualitative teaching signal.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of dopamine recovery slopes with interpretation of functional significance.

claim: When WN duration deviates from expected, dopamine concentration reflects only the duration of WN exposure, but not a prediction error.
source: Thus, when our rats were exposed to unexpectedly extended WN or to the unexpected omission of WN, dopamine concentration reflected only the duration of WN exposure, but not a prediction error.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis of dopamine responses to extended and omitted WN trials.

claim: Dopamine can encode rewards during ongoing WN exposure, showing a significant increase upon pellet delivery comparable to pellet delivery without WN.
source: We observed a significant increase in dopamine release upon pellet delivery (t(5) = 3.108, p=0.0266, Figure 3G), which was comparable to the increase in dopamine release we observed upon pellet delivery in the absence of WN (t(5) = 0.08753, p=0.9336, Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by FSCV measurements during concurrent reward and WN presentation with statistical analysis.

claim: Dopamine integrates information about appetitive and aversive events in an additive manner.
source: These results indicate that dopamine is still responsive to rewarding events during an aversive event and, thus, integrates information about appetitive and aversive events.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that reward-induced dopamine increase occurs during WN-induced dopamine decrease.

claim: Reward context (probability of intermittent reward delivery) does not significantly affect dopamine concentration during cue or WN epochs.
source: We did not observe a significant difference in dopamine concentration between these reward contexts during the cue epoch (t(5) = 0.2841, p=0.7877), nor during the WN epoch (t(5) = 0.3151, p=0.7654) (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of FSCV data between different reward context conditions.

claim: NAC dopamine primarily tracks prediction and duration of aversive events rather than encoding an aversive prediction error.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that instead of an APE, NAC dopamine primarily tracks prediction and duration of aversive events.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Dopamine responses to simultaneous presentation of rewarding and aversive stimuli are additive despite differing signal qualities.
source: Despite differing signal qualities, dopamine responses to simultaneous presentation of rewarding and aversive stimuli were additive.
evidence: Based on experimental observations of dopamine responses to concurrent reward and WN presentation.

claim: Unpredicted WN provokes slower post-stimulus signal recovery than predicted WN.
source: However, unpredicted WN provoked slower post-stimulus signal recovery than predicted WN.
evidence: Based on analysis of dopamine recovery slopes comparing predicted and unpredicted WN.

claim: The dopamine signal during aversive conditioning is unaffected by WN value, context valence, or probabilistic contingencies.
source: In contrast to reward conditioning, this dopamine signal was unaffected by WN value, context valence, or probabilistic contingencies
evidence: Based on multiple experiments testing these variables and finding no significant effects on dopamine.

claim: The WN dopamine response shifts only partially toward its predictive cue, unlike the complete shift observed in reward conditioning.
source: and the WN dopamine response shifted only partially toward its predictive cue.
evidence: Based on comparison of temporal dynamics between aversive and appetitive conditioning.

claim: Both WN and its predictive cue induce a negative dopamine ramp, followed by slow signal recovery upon stimulus cessation.
source: Both induced a negative dopamine ramp, followed by slow signal recovery upon stimulus cessation.
evidence: Based on FSCV measurements showing the temporal profile of dopamine changes.

claim: The midbrain dopamine system plays critical roles in motivation, learning, and movement, specifically for learning about rewards and creating motivational states that promote reward-seeking.
source: The midbrain dopamine system plays critical roles in motivation, learning, and movement; specifically for learning about rewards and creating motivational states that promote reward-seeking (Berridge and Robinson, 1998; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Berke, 2018; Schultz, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Dopamine neurons encode a reward prediction error (RPE) signal, where dopamine cell firing and terminal release shifts backward in time from reward delivery to cue presentation when a reward is fully predicted.
source: One of the most prominent functions of dopamine is the encoding of a so-called reward prediction error (RPE) signal (Schultz et al., 1997): when a reward is fully predicted by a cue, the increase in dopamine cell firing and terminal release of dopamine shifts 'backward' in time from the moment of reward delivery, to that of cue presentation (Schultz et al., 1997; Flagel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to seminal studies on dopamine and reward prediction error.

claim: Dopamine neurons pause their firing when a predicted reward is omitted and increase their firing in response to delivery of an unpredicted reward.
source: Furthermore, dopamine neurons pause their firing when a predicted reward is omitted and increase their firing in response to the delivery of an unpredicted reward.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of dopamine neuron firing patterns in reward prediction error.

claim: Dopamine neuron activity scales with the relative value of reward and unexpected deviations from this value.
source: Thus, dopamine neurons encode the difference between predicted and obtained reward, which is corroborated by the fact that dopamine neuron activity scales with the relative value of reward and unexpected deviations from this value (Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on dopamine encoding of reward value.

claim: Reports on the effect of aversive events on the dopamine system are less consistent than those for rewards, with studies showing inhibition, excitation, or no effect on dopamine neuron activity.
source: In contrast to the primarily stimulatory response of rewards on dopamine activity, the reports on the effect of aversive events on the dopamine system are less consistent. For example, on the level of dopamine neuron cell bodies, aversive stimuli were demonstrated to result in inhibition of neuronal activity (Ungless et al., 2004; Mileykovskiy and Morales, 2011), excitation thereof (Anstrom et al., 2009; Valenti et al., 2011), or no effect at all (Mirenowicz and Schultz, 1996; Fiorillo, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing contradictory findings.

claim: Subpopulations of dopamine neurons exhibit different response profiles to aversive stimuli.
source: The widely accepted explanation for these varying results is that subpopulations of dopamine neurons exhibit different response profiles to aversive stimuli (Schultz and Romo, 1987; Guarraci and Kapp, 1999; Coizet et al., 2006; Bromberg-Martin and Hikosaka, 2009; Zweifel et al., 2011; Cohen et al., 2012; Lammel et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on heterogeneity of dopamine neuron responses.

claim: Activity at the level of dopamine neuron cell bodies does not necessarily always translate to their projection targets.
source: However, activity at the level of dopamine neuron cell bodies does not necessarily always translate to their projection targets (Mohebi et al., 2019) as axonal terminal release of dopamine may be capable of operating independently from cell body activity (Threlfell et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing dissociation between cell body activity and terminal release.

claim: Dopamine signals display regional heterogeneity across the striatum, inconsistent with the hypothesis of a uniform signal broadcast.
source: Inconsistent with the classic hypothesis positing that the dopamine system broadcasts a uniform signal across the striatum, it has been reported multiple times in recent years that dopamine signals display regional heterogeneity (Willuhn et al., 2012; Willuhn et al., 2014a, Lammel et al., 2011; de Jong et al., 2019; Menegas et al., 2017; Klanker et al., 2017; van Elzelingen et al., 2022a; van Elzelingen et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple recent studies demonstrating regional differences.

claim: Microdialysis studies report an increase in dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in response to aversive events.
source: whereas microdialysis studies report an increase in dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in response to aversive events (Young et al., 1993; Young, 2004; Wilkinson et al., 1998; Bassareo et al., 2002; Pascucci et al., 2007; Ventura et al., 2007; Martinez et al., 2008 but see Mark et al., 1991; Liu et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to microdialysis studies, with some exceptions noted.

claim: Studies using subsecond temporal resolution techniques arrive at less consistent conclusions about dopamine responses to aversive stimuli in the nucleus accumbens.
source: studies employing techniques with a higher, subsecond temporal resolution (e.g., fast-scan cyclic voltammetry [FSCV] or fluorescence fiber photometry) arrive at less consistent conclusions.
evidence: Based on review of literature using different measurement techniques.

claim: Aversive stimuli produce both increases and decreases in dopaminergic activity in the nucleus accumbens shell (NAS) depending on the study.
source: For example, aversive stimuli produced an increase in dopaminergic activity in the nucleus accumbens shell (NAS) in some studies (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019), but a decrease in others (Roitman et al., 2008; Wheeler et al., 2011; McCutcheon et al., 2012; Twining et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies with contradictory findings.

claim: Contradictory findings of both increased and decreased dopamine activity in response to aversive stimuli are reported in the nucleus accumbens core (NAC).
source: Similarly, contradictory findings are also reported in the neighboring nucleus accumbens core (NAC), where studies found both increased (Budygin et al., 2012; Mikhailova et al., 2019; Kutlu et al., 2021; Kutlu et al., 2022) and decreased dopamine activity (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019; Stelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies with contradictory findings in NAC.

claim: In the tail of the striatum, aversive events exclusively result in increased dopaminergic activity.
source: In contrast, in the tail of the striatum, aversive events exclusively result in increased dopaminergic activity (Menegas et al., 2017; Menegas et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on the tail of the striatum.

claim: Most studies observe a change in dopaminergic activity in response to aversive stimuli, with substantial differences between striatal regions.
source: Overall, it can be concluded that most studies observe a change in dopaminergic activity in response to aversive stimuli, that there are substantial differences between striatal regions in this response, and that it remains unclear what determines whether aversive events provoke an increase or a decrease in dopaminergic activity within striatal regions.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from review of literature on regional dopamine responses.

claim: Some studies have observed aspects of a dopamine aversive prediction error (APE), such as predictive cues adopting the dopamine response of aversive stimuli.
source: other studies have observed aspects of a dopamine APE, such as the predictive cue adopting the dopamine response of an aversive stimulus (Guarraci and Kapp, 1999; Oleson et al., 2012; Badrinarayan et al., 2012), or an APE-like response when the aversive stimulus was unpredicted or omitted (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2016; Menegas et al., 2017; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing APE-like features.

claim: In cases of omission or early termination of an expected aversive event, rewarding aspects of a milder-than-expected event (RPE) may be mixed with an APE.
source: However, it should be kept in mind that in case of omission or early termination of an expected aversive event, rewarding aspects of a milder-than-expected aversive event (RPE) may be mixed with an APE (Oleson et al., 2012; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Stelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference about confounding factors in APE interpretation.

claim: The NAC is a hotspot for reward prediction error (RPE)-like signals and is tightly linked to motivational processes related to aversion avoidance.
source: Using FSCV, we measured the NAC dopamine response to these conditions since the NAC is a hotspot for RPE-like signals (Flagel et al., 2011; Papageorgiou et al., 2016) and is also tightly linked to motivational processes related to aversion avoidance (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Stelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on NAC function in reward and aversion.

claim: White noise (WN) possesses several merits as an aversive stimulus: it is well-tolerated, not painful, precisely controllable, aversive without inducing freezing, does not jeopardize recording equipment, does not introduce artifacts, and can be administered reliably.
source: WN possesses several merits as it is well-tolerated by rats and is not painful, precisely controllable (intensity and duration can be effortlessly titrated), aversive without inducing freezing (most pertinent to this study as this might interfere with the dopamine signal), does not jeopardize the recording equipment, does not introduce artifacts to the recordings, and can be administered reliably (see 'Discussion').
evidence: Based on the authors' experimental experience and rationale for stimulus choice.

claim: WN at intensities not prone to cause hearing loss is moderately aversive and does not induce freezing but provokes mild behavioral activation.
source: First, at intensities that are not prone to cause loss of hearing (Escabi et al., 2019), WN is moderately aversive (Campbell and Bloom, 1965; Hughes and Bardo, 1981), and as such does not induce freezing, but instead provokes mild behavioral activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on WN effects and hearing safety.

claim: Lack of movement is often associated with diminished activity of the dopamine system, which may confound interpretation of negative dopamine signals in the context of aversive events.
source: This is particularly relevant with regard to studies relating dopamine function to behavioral read-outs since lack of movement is often associated with diminished activity of the dopamine system and, thus, may confound the interpretation of negative dopamine signals in the context of aversive events.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of dopamine-movement relationships and logical inference about confounds.

claim: The behavioral activation observed in response to WN might reflect an increased motivation to escape.
source: The behavioral activation we observe in response to WN might reflect an increased motivation to escape, which we cannot ascertain as our task was Pavlovian (thus, without an active avoidance component: the WN was inescapable).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of behavioral observations with acknowledgment of experimental limitations.

claim: During mild WN exposure, NAC dopamine may be uncoupled from its usual, more direct behavioral impact.
source: Notably, the observed decline in dopamine was not at all correlated with movement on a trial-by-trial basis; thus, it is conceivable that during mild WN exposure, NAC dopamine was uncoupled from its usual, more direct behavioral impact.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the lack of correlation between dopamine and movement.

claim: NAC dopamine does not fulfill the axiomatic criteria of an aversive prediction error (APE) when aversive stimulus intensity or value is varied.
source: Thus, we conclude that the NAC dopamine signals we observed did not fulfill the axiomatic criteria of an APE, when aversive stimulus intensity or value was varied.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from applying mathematical framework to experimental data.

claim: NAC dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration.
source: In summary, we conclude that dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with varying WN durations.

claim: The only evidence of an APE-like signal in the data was found after unpredicted WN.
source: and the only evidence of an APE-like signal in our data was found after unpredicted WN
evidence: Summary of findings regarding prediction error signals.

claim: Several experimental accounts are incompatible with an APE function of NAC dopamine.
source: whereas several of our other experimental accounts are incompatible with an APE function of NAC dopamine.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claim: NAC dopamine encodes both reward and aversive prediction.
source: Taken together, this suggests that NAC dopamine encodes both reward and aversive prediction.
evidence: Inference drawn from observations of dopamine responses to predictive cues.

claim: Decreases in dopamine concentration do not scale with WN intensity, unlike reward processing where reward size or probability is encoded.
source: However, decreases in dopamine concentration did not scale with WN intensity, unlike what is well-established for reward processing, where reward size or probability is encoded both for the reward itself and for predictive stimuli (Gan et al., 2010; Tobler et al., 2005; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison of current findings with established literature on reward encoding.

claim: The diminishing effect of WN on NAC dopamine may be related to pre-attentive processes involved in saliency and novelty, dissociable from NAC value signals.
source: Thus, one could speculate that the diminishing effect of WN on NAC dopamine may be related to pre-attentive processes involved in saliency and novelty – dissociable from NAC value signals (Redgrave and Gurney, 2006; Kutlu et al., 2021; Kutlu et al., 2022).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: NAC dopamine does not encode aversive and appetitive stimuli (and their prediction) in the same way.
source: Thus, NAC dopamine does not encode aversive and appetitive stimuli (and their prediction) in the same way.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of aversive and appetitive conditioning data.

claim: The basic nature of aversion-related dopamine signals is different from that of rewards, with larger and faster changes for rewards compared to aversive events.
source: Moreover, the basic nature of aversion-related dopamine signals in our data was different from that of rewards. For example, the temporal signal shift toward the earliest predictor of the respective reinforcing stimulus, as described for rewards, is incomplete for aversive conditioning. Another example is that reward-related changes in extracellular dopamine concentration are substantially larger and faster compared to aversive events.
evidence: Based on comparison of temporal and magnitude characteristics between reward and aversion signals.

claim: The dopamine system has a bigger dynamic range for increasing activity compared to decreasing activity, which may be a structurally limiting factor on what can be encoded by dopamine reduction.
source: More specifically, the dopamine system presumably has a bigger dynamic range for increasing activity; it can do so, for example, by increasing the number of cells firing and their firing frequency (and thereby the total number of dopamine-containing vesicles being released). In contrast, dopamine-signaling reduction cannot drop below a certain point since the cells' maximum response is to cease firing altogether and extracellular dopamine can only be removed relatively slowly or must diffuse away. This disparity could translate into a structurally limiting factor on what can be encoded by a reduction in dopamine concentration and explain some of the abovementioned differences in function.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic explanation based on known physiology of dopamine neurons.

claim: The slow-ramping declining and recovery slopes observed do not reflect system limits, as evidenced by steeper changes in other conditions.
source: However, the slow-ramping declining and recovery slopes we observed do not reflect the system limits since the very first exposure to WN resulted in a steeper decline and rewards given during WN resulted in steeper increases.
evidence: Based on comparison of dopamine dynamics across different experimental conditions.

claim: Aversive events are encoded by NAC dopamine more rudimentarily in a qualitative instead of quantitative fashion.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that there are a few similarities between dopamine encoding of rewards and aversive stimuli, but overall we found more differences between them – hinting at aversive events being encoded by NAC dopamine more rudimentarily in a qualitative instead of quantitative fashion.
evidence: Summary interpretation of findings comparing reward and aversion encoding.

claim: WN is a valuable and versatile aversive stimulus well-suited to probe how the brain processes aversive stimuli.
source: In summary, our findings demonstrate that WN is a valuable and versatile aversive stimulus that is well-suited to probe how the brain processes aversive stimuli.
evidence: Summary conclusion about the utility of WN as an experimental tool.

claim: Dopamine tracks the anticipation and duration of an aversive event as a perpetually declining dopamine ramp that progresses without altering its slope until offset of the aversive stimulus.
source: Overall, we conclude that dopamine tracks the anticipation and duration of an aversive event. This tracking materializes as a perpetually declining dopamine ramp that progresses without altering its slope until offset of the aversive stimulus (even WN lasting for 24 s did not reach a plateau of minimal dopamine concentration).
evidence: Summary of findings on temporal dynamics of dopamine during aversive events.

claim: Slowly ramping aversion signals may play an anticipatory role for certain defensive behaviors since animals were behaviorally activated during the aversive event.
source: Such aversion tracking may play an anticipatory role for certain defensive behaviors since the animals were behaviorally activated during the aversive event.
evidence: Speculative functional interpretation based on observed behavioral activation.

claim: Slowly ramping aversion signals may contribute to a qualitative learning signal rather than a quantitative or scalar APE signal.
source: Furthermore, we speculate that these slowly ramping aversion signals may contribute to a qualitative learning signal (other than a quantitative or scalar APE signal) since the unexpected aversive stimulus elicited a response beyond simply tracking the stimulus.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on differential response to unpredicted WN.

claim: Dopamine tracks both positive and negative valence in their temporal aspects and prediction, but exact value and error is only encoded for rewards in the upward direction of NAC dopamine concentration.
source: Thus, we conclude that dopamine tracks both positive and negative valence in their temporal aspects and prediction, but that quantitatively speaking, the exact value and error is only encoded for rewards, in the upward direction of NAC dopamine concentration.
evidence: Summary conclusion integrating findings on reward and aversion encoding.

claim: Aversive value and aversive prediction errors (APEs) are encoded in other brain regions, not in NAC dopamine.
source: This implies that aversive value and APEs are encoded in other brain regions.
evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of APE encoding in NAC dopamine.

claim: Increased locomotion speed associated with decreased dopamine release during WN exposure represents a rare relationship between dopamine and behavior.
source: Interestingly, the use of WN revealed a rare relationship between dopamine and behavior: increased locomotion speed was associated with a decrease in dopamine release.
evidence: Based on observed dissociation between typical dopamine-behavior relationships.

claim: Behavioral activation is usually associated with increased dopamine signaling, while lack of movement or freezing is associated with decreased dopamine.
source: Behavioral activation is usually associated with increased dopamine signaling (Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Berridge and Robinson, 1998; da Silva et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2019), whereas a lack of movement or even freezing, depending on stimulus intensity, is often associated with decreased dopamine (e.g., Oleson et al., 2012; Badrinarayan et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopamine-behavior relationships.

claim: The hypothesis that directionality of changes in dopamine concentration reflects the chosen behavioral strategy (active or passive) when confronted with aversive stimuli is not universally applicable.
source: These frequently observed association patterns have prompted the hypothesis that the directionality of changes in dopamine concentration reflects the chosen behavioral strategy when confronted with aversive stimuli: an active or a passive reaction (Badrinarayan et al., 2012). Our results, however, prove that this hypothesis is not universally applicable.
evidence: Based on current findings contradicting the cited hypothesis.

claim: Freezing elicited via electric shocks is accompanied by decreased NAC dopamine activity.
source: Freezing elicited via electric shocks is accompanied by decreased NAC dopamine activity (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019; Stelly et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopamine responses to shock-induced freezing.

claim: During mild WN exposure, NAC dopamine decline was not correlated with movement on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: Notably, the observed decline in dopamine was not at all correlated with movement on a trial-by-trial basis
evidence: Based on regression analysis showing no correlation.

claim: Fiorillo (2013) concluded that dopamine is insensitive to aversiveness based on three criteria: no difference between aversive and neutral stimuli, no effect of prediction, and no integration of rewarding and aversive values.
source: Their conclusions range from 'dopamine is insensitive to aversiveness' (Fiorillo, 2013), to the other extreme of 'dopamine serves as an APE' (Matsumoto et al., 2016). Fiorillo, 2013 ruled out the existence of a dopamine APE because (1) dopamine-neuron firing did not differ between presentation of aversive and neutral stimuli, (2) prediction of an aversive event did not affect firing, and (3) no integration of rewarding and aversive values was observed.
evidence: Summary of conclusions from cited study.

claim: Matsumoto et al. (2016) found evidence for all three requirements of an APE and concluded that dopamine neurons encode a value prediction error equally for both rewards and aversive stimuli.
source: In contrast, Matsumoto et al., 2016 found evidence for all three of these requirements and, therefore, concluded that dopamine neurons are capable of encoding a value prediction error (equally for both rewards and aversive stimuli).
evidence: Summary of conclusions from cited study.

claim: The discrepancy between Fiorillo (2013) and Matsumoto et al. (2016) could be partially explained by recording from different brain regions (substantia nigra vs. VTA) and different species (monkeys vs. mice).
source: This discrepancy could partially be explained by the fact that Matsumoto et al., 2016 recorded from dopaminergic neurons in the VTA (of mice), whereas the majority of the neurons that Fiorillo, 2013 recorded were in the substantia nigra (of monkeys).
evidence: Inference about methodological differences explaining contradictory findings.

claim: NAC dopamine is released from terminals that originate from neurons in the VTA.
source: Since we measured extracellular concentrations of NAC dopamine, which is released from terminals that originate from neurons in the VTA (Ikemoto, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical literature.

claim: Context was irrelevant to the magnitude of dopamine response to aversive events and rewards in the current study.
source: although a noteworthy contrast is that in our data, context was irrelevant to the magnitude of dopamine response to the aversive event and reward: it made no difference for the acute dopamine response magnitude whether the aversive stimulus was delivered in rewarding contexts or not.
evidence: Based on experimental findings comparing different reward contexts.

claim: The NAC dopamine signals observed did not fulfill the axiomatic criteria of an APE when aversive stimulus intensity or value was varied, as tested using the mathematical approach of Caplin and Dean (2007).
source: Next, however, we took inspiration from Hart et al., 2014, who used a mathematical approach developed by Caplin and Dean, 2007 to confirm the encoding of RPE signals by NAC dopamine. They used a deterministic and a probabilistic choice task in order to determine whether dopamine signals fulfilled three axioms that were considered necessary for a RPE signal: 'consistent prize ordering,' 'consistent lottery ordering,' and 'no surprise equivalence.' We employed the abovementioned deterministic and probabilistic Pavlovian conditioning tasks to identify an APE, instead of an RPE, by exposing rats to low- and high-dB WN, predicted by two different tones, with either a 100% probability (deterministic task) or with different probabilities (probabilistic task).
evidence: Based on application of mathematical framework to experimental data.

claim: The third axiom (no surprise equivalence) was fulfilled since no differences in dopamine were observed during the WN epoch in the deterministic task.
source: We did not observe differences in dopamine concentration during the WN epoch in the deterministic task, which fulfills the third axiom (no surprise equivalence), since the prediction error is zero for both of these conditions.
evidence: Based on analysis of deterministic task data in relation to axiomatic criteria.

claim: The first two axioms (consistent prize ordering and consistent lottery ordering) were not fulfilled since no differences in dopamine were detected when different WN intensities were presented with different probabilities.
source: But the first two axioms were not fulfilled since we did not detect differences in dopamine during the WN epoch, when different WN intensities were presented with different probabilities.
evidence: Based on analysis of probabilistic task data in relation to axiomatic criteria.

claim: Rats avoided higher-dB WN more than lower-dB WN and exhibited WN dB-dependent locomotor activation, indicating that WN aversiveness scales with intensity and rats can discriminate between intensities.
source: Rats avoided higher-dB WN more than lower-dB WN (Figure 1B) and exhibited WN dB-dependent locomotor activation (Figure 2F), indicating that WN aversiveness scales with WN intensity and that rats are able to discriminate between different WN intensities.
evidence: Based on behavioral data from multiple experiments.

claim: NAC dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration, as evidenced by continuation of declining dopamine slope during extended WN and prompt cessation at WN offset.
source: Extended WN elicited a continuation of the same declining dopamine concentration slope, which ceased promptly at WN cessation, after which dopamine slowly ramped backup toward baseline with a reversed, inclining slope. Thus, although the signal reflected the duration of extended WN, no discernible error component was evident.
evidence: Based on FSCV measurements during extended WN trials.

claim: When WN was omitted, no error signal was observed; instead, the dopamine signal slowly returned to baseline levels.
source: When WN was omitted, we did not observe an error signal either: instead, again, the signal slowly returned to baseline levels.
evidence: Based on FSCV measurements during WN omission trials.

claim: NAC dopamine signals more than simply tracking the presence of aversive stimuli, as evidenced by the differential recovery slope after unpredicted WN.
source: This flattened recovery slope indicates that NAC dopamine signals more than simply track the presence of aversive stimuli; in addition, it may relate to the failed anticipation of an aversive event (based on reliance on the predictive cue), and, thus, indicate altered cue-WN contingencies.
evidence: Interpretation of differential recovery slope as indicating additional signaling beyond stimulus tracking.

claim: NAC dopamine encodes rewarding and aversive events with opposite directionality, consistent with most literature.
source: Consistent with most literature (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019; Stelly et al., 2019), we found that NAC dopamine encodes rewarding and aversive events with opposite directionality.
evidence: Based on comparison of dopamine responses to rewards and aversive stimuli, supported by citations.

claim: A cue predicting an aversive stimulus can adopt the ability to prompt dopamine changes the way the aversive stimulus itself would.
source: Furthermore, we report that a cue predicting an aversive stimulus can adopt the ability to prompt dopamine changes the way the aversive stimulus itself would.
evidence: Based on observations of conditioned dopamine responses to predictive cues.

claim: Reward size or probability is encoded by dopamine both for the reward itself and for predictive stimuli.
source: However, decreases in dopamine concentration did not scale with WN intensity, unlike what is well-established for reward processing, where reward size or probability is encoded both for the reward itself and for predictive stimuli (Gan et al., 2010; Tobler et al., 2005; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on reward encoding.

claim: Encoding of a prediction error is one of the best-characterized features of reward-related dopamine signaling.
source: Furthermore, encoding of a prediction error, which is one of the best-characterized features of reward-related dopamine signaling, did not occur for aversive events.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of dopamine function in reward processing.

claim: The temporal signal shift toward the earliest predictor of the reinforcing stimulus, as described for rewards, is incomplete for aversive conditioning.
source: For example, the temporal signal shift toward the earliest predictor of the respective reinforcing stimulus, as described for rewards, is incomplete for aversive conditioning.
evidence: Based on comparison of temporal dynamics between reward and aversive conditioning.

claim: Reward-related changes in extracellular dopamine concentration are substantially larger and faster compared to aversive events.
source: Another example is that reward-related changes in extracellular dopamine concentration are substantially larger and faster compared to aversive events.
evidence: Based on comparison of magnitude and kinetics of dopamine changes.

claim: Disparate qualitative differences were found in NAC-dopamine responses to the presentation of ultrasonic vocalizations associated with rewarding and aversive events.
source: Furthermore, disparate qualitative differences were also found in NAC-dopamine responses to the presentation of ultrasonic vocalizations that are associated with rewarding and aversive events (Willuhn et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on dopamine responses to vocalizations.

claim: There are more differences than similarities between dopamine encoding of rewards and aversive stimuli, hinting at aversive events being encoded more rudimentarily in a qualitative fashion.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that there are a few similarities between dopamine encoding of rewards and aversive stimuli, but overall we found more differences between them – hinting at aversive events being encoded by NAC dopamine more rudimentarily in a qualitative instead of quantitative fashion.
evidence: Summary interpretation of comparative findings.

claim: Even WN lasting for 24 s did not reach a plateau of minimal dopamine concentration.
source: This tracking materializes as a perpetually declining dopamine ramp that progresses without altering its slope until offset of the aversive stimulus (even WN lasting for 24 s did not reach a plateau of minimal dopamine concentration).
evidence: Based on FSCV measurements during prolonged WN exposure.

claim: The unexpected aversive stimulus elicited a response beyond simply tracking the stimulus, suggesting contribution to a qualitative learning signal.
source: Furthermore, we speculate that these slowly ramping aversion signals may contribute to a qualitative learning signal (other than a quantitative or scalar APE signal) since the unexpected aversive stimulus elicited a response beyond simply tracking the stimulus.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on differential response to unpredicted WN.
